strengths: Addresses a relevant question: what multimodal contrastive learning can recover when modalities contain distinct but statistically coupled latent factors.

The empirical coverage is broad, including synthetic assumption violations, four CLIP backbones, ImageNet distribution shifts, and 11 few-shot datasets. The inexpensive postprocessing pipelines show useful improvements over several reported baselines.
Synthetic experiments include repeated runs and ground-truth recovery metrics. The additional Multimodal3DIdent experiment provides evidence beyond qualitative latent traversals.
weaknesses: The central proofs rely on a false lemma. Appendix D.1, Lemma 2 claims that the normalized contrastive objective has global minimum zero. Collapsed encoders already achieve zero, whereas a realizable density-ratio score for informative pairs achieves -2I(x;t)<0. Furthermore, almost-sure equality of positive-pair embeddings under the full-support vMF conditional forces constant representations, contradicting the lemma's uniform-output condition. Both Theorems 4.1 and 4.2 depend on this argument, leaving the main identifiability guarantees unsupported.

The convex-body analysis has additional substantive errors. Appendix E.1 uses an exactly uniform text marginal, although Lemma 3 establishes uniformity only as lambda approaches zero. At finite lambda, boundary-dependent normalization generally makes that marginal nonuniform, invalidating the stated cross-entropy reduction. Corollary 2 also omits the restriction to L_alpha geometry with alpha different from 2 used in its proof; arbitrary rotations remain ambiguous on a Euclidean ball.

The claimed FastICA guarantee conflicts with the spherical assumptions. Coordinates of a uniformly distributed point on a sphere are dependent because their squared values sum to one, and rotational symmetry prevents identifying a preferred ICA orientation. Having M-1 intrinsic dimensions does not resolve this incompatibility. Appendix O additionally treats arbitrary orthogonal mixing as component-wise disentanglement, conflating linear recoverability with factor separation. The proposed PCA remedy for the geometry mismatch is heuristic.

The downstream experiments do not isolate the claimed disentanglement mechanism. FastICA introduces whitening and dimensionality reduction, but dimension-matched PCA-only and whitening controls are missing. An orthogonal rotation after fixed whitening leaves an optimally fitted L2-regularized linear probe invariant. Consequently, improved classification accuracy cannot establish that independent-component recovery caused the gains.

The recovery evaluation overstates its conclusions. Appendix K regresses learned representations on true factors; a rank-deficient projection that discards factors can still achieve perfect R-squared in this direction. Multimodal3DIdent R-squared establishes linear predictability rather than component-wise disentanglement. CelebA evidence consists primarily of selected traversals without quantitative factor-isolation measurements or controlled baseline comparisons.

The causal novelty is insufficiently established. An undirected dependence between latent blocks does not specify intervention semantics, and the proposed distributions still factor as p(z_x)p(z_t|z_x). Neither the theory nor experiments demonstrate a particular advantage for mixtures of opposing causal mechanisms. Much of the geometric identifiability machinery is explicitly inherited from Zimmermann et al. (2021), making the invalid multimodal reduction especially consequential.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement: real-data comparisons lack uncertainty estimates, important synthetic and Multimodal3DIdent training details are missing, and the reproducibility statement defers code release. Table 2 also contains a material arithmetic error: the RN101 baseline target accuracies average 22.03%, whereas 20.03% is reported, exaggerating the apparent improvement.
